cycles.name: Foundation Forge
focuses: Build foundational strength and movement quality across all major patterns.
Establish movement patterns that counteract tennis-specific postural imbalances.
Develop scapular stability and posterior chain strength as injury-prevention anchors.
Introduce reactive plyometric work to build tendon elasticity and court-transfer qualities.

cycles.name: Strength Engine
focuses: Progressive strength overload across all major patterns with knee and shoulder injury management.
Intensify scapular stability and posterior chain work as injury-prevention anchors.

cycles.name: Power Transfer
focuses: Convert built strength into court-relevant power — rotational, reactive, and unilateral.
Reinforce shoulder girdle resilience under higher velocity demands.

paragraphs: Mehraneh, the first ten weeks were about building something worth using. You did that — the squat went from 10 kilograms to 50 while your knees stayed quiet. The shoulder that was a 6 out of 10 in Week 1 hasn't been mentioned since Week 2. The foundation is real. This cycle is where it becomes athletic.

Power Transfer has one job: take the strength you built and teach your body to express it fast. The med-ball throws, the box jumps, the speed pulls — these aren't harder versions of what you've been doing. They're a different quality altogether. The shift you need to make mentally is from pushing hard to moving fast. Every repetition of every power exercise has one cue that overrides all others: intent. A slow throw is a wasted rep.

By the end of these five weeks, you will feel a difference on the court before you see one in the gym. First steps, change of direction, the moment you load a forehand — these are the outputs. The gym work is the input.
outcomes: Reactive jump landings controlled and pain-free under load
Rotational throw velocity visibly faster side to side
Squat at 5 reps heavy — moved with intent, not grind
Landmine push press progressed past the 5 kg OHP wall
Trap-bar speed pulls feeling explosive, not effortful
Day 4 completed every week without exception

cycles.name: Power Reload
focuses: Rebuild barbell strength with a rep scheme that actually lets the load climb.
Build an upper back that holds up through a heavy week on court.
Three sessions a week, every week, with the conditioning built into one of them.
Lift the readiness score by fixing one thing about sleep.

paragraphs: Mehraneh, your knees and your shoulders are clear. Both of them. Back in May a knee was 5 out of 10 and your right shoulder was a 6, and you haven't mentioned either one since. You jumped, you bounded and you pressed overhead all cycle and nothing complained. That chapter is closed.

What didn't move is the bar. Your squat sat on the same weight for ten weeks and your trap bar actually went down. That's on how it was written, not on you. Five reps with a slow lowering was never going to let the weight climb. So this cycle cuts the reps and takes the slow part out, and the same effort will land on a heavier bar.

Three days now instead of four. Your logs told me four doesn't happen, so the fourth day is gone and the conditioning lives inside day three. And day two is rebuilt around the one thing that still bothers you, that upper back after a heavy week of playing. A lot more pulling, much less pressing. That's the fix.
outcomes: Squat moving again after ten weeks stuck
Trap bar pulled clean and controlled every week, heavy rebuild deferred
Three sessions a week, every week
An upper back that survives a heavy playing week
Your first unassisted pull-up in sight
One sleep habit held all five weeks

cycles.name: Performance Peak
focuses: Sharpen athletic output — speed, reactive strength, and sport-specific conditioning.
Sustain structural integrity under competition load; refine movement economy.

paragraphs: Cycle 5 is the one you've been building toward since May. The speed gets tested. The reactions get tested. The engine gets pushed to its ceiling and asked to hold it there.
Nothing gets rebuilt after this. What you bring into it is what you play with.
Earn it in these five weeks.

cycles.name: Armor & Maintain
focuses: Maintain peak strength while reducing injury risk heading into high-competition periods.
Optimize recovery capacity and tissue resilience for the long season.

days.completionMessage: That's the squat unstuck and the legs springing again. Eat something with protein in the next hour and let the legs settle.

good: Easy, building pace, just raise the temperature
Legs warming and breathing opening
bad: Don't make this a workout, it's a primer

good: Take both knees to the floor on each side
Feel the stretch deep in the hip
bad: Don't let the chest collapse forward

good: Sit into one hip and keep the other leg straight
Feel the inner thigh lengthen
bad: Don't let the heel lift off the floor

good: Drive the knee forward past the toes
Feel the stretch behind the ankle
bad: Don't let the heel come up

exercises.name: Reactive Circuit

good: Jump for distance and land like you meant it
Feel the hips snap open
bad: Don't land stiff-legged

good: Push off sideways and stick the landing dead still
Feel the outside of the hip catch you
bad: Don't let the knee fall inward on landing

good: Stay on the balls of the feet and get off the floor fast
Feel the calves and ankles springing
bad: Don't bend the knees deep between jumps

exercises.note: Staying exactly as it was. Your jumps are not the problem here and I am not taking them off you. Same rule as before, every landing silent and still before the next rep. Land soft through the hips, do not catch it in the low back.

exercises.name: Barbell Back Squat

good: Drive the floor away from you
Feel the weight through the middle of the foot and the glutes
bad: Don't let the knees cave in as you stand up

exercises.note: Stay on the weight you did last session. No jump this week or next while your back settles, and that is not the program stalling, it is one deliberate pause. Brace before you unrack and keep the ribs down out of the hole. If the low back talks on a set, that is the end of the exercise, not the end of the session.

exercises.name: Barbell Hip Thrust

good: Push the floor away through your heels
Feel the glutes doing all the work at the top
bad: Don't arch the low back to finish the rep
Don't hold the squeeze at the top, come straight back down

exercises.note: The hold at the top is gone while your back settles. Come up to a straight line from knee to shoulder and come straight back down. Ribs stay down, chin stays tucked. If you feel it in your low back instead of your glutes, you have gone too high.

good: Keep your weight over the front foot the whole set
Feel the front thigh and glute stretch under load
bad: Don't let the front knee drift inward

exercises.name: Copenhagen Plank

good: Press the bottom knee into the bench and lift the hips
Feel the inner thigh of the top leg working
bad: Don't let the hips sag toward the floor

exercises.note: You logged this at a 10 when the card said 7, so the hold comes down to fifteen seconds. Same three sets. Keep the bottom knee on the bench, not the ankle. When the hips start to sag the set is over, even if there is time left on the clock.

days.completionMessage: Every one of those pulls is what keeps your upper back quiet after a long week on court. Get your shoulders out of the forward position for the rest of the day.

good: Smooth, steady pulls
Shoulders and back warming up
bad: Don't yank with the arms only

good: Pull the band apart out to the sides
Feel the muscles between the shoulder blades
bad: Don't shrug the shoulders up

good: Keep the forearms on the wall the whole way
Feel the shoulder blades slide down and back
bad: Don't let the low back peel off the wall

good: Open the top arm all the way back toward the floor
Feel the mid-back and chest open up
bad: Don't let the knees roll and twist from the low back

exercises.name: Single-Arm Landmine Push Press

good: Dip the legs and drive the bar up in one move
Feel the legs start it and the shoulder finish it
bad: Don't press with the arm alone, no leg drive
Don't lean back and arch to finish the rep

exercises.note: You went from 2.5 kg to 5 kg on this last cycle without a word from your shoulder. Fewer reps and a harder target this time, so 5 kg should be your floor here, not your ceiling.

exercises.name: Machine Assisted Pull-Up

good: Pull your chest toward the bar
Feel it in the lats, under the armpits
bad: Don't swing the legs to get up

exercises.note: You pull 45 kg for 8 on the pulldown, so this is well within reach. Set the assistance so the sixth rep is hard but still clean. The goal by the end of this cycle is less help on the machine, and eventually none.

exercises.name: Cable Seated Row

good: Pull the handle to your belly button
Feel the shoulder blades squeeze together
bad: Don't rock backward to move the weight

exercises.note: Four sets, not three. This is the main piece of work for your upper back, so it doesn't get cut on a rushed day.

exercises.name: Cable Face Pull

good: Pull the rope to your forehead and split your hands apart
Feel the back of the shoulders and between the blades
bad: Don't let the elbows drop below shoulder height

exercises.note: This one is in the program specifically for the ache you get after a heavy week of playing. It trains the exact muscles that give up when you serve and hit overheads for hours. Light weight, slow, and feel it.

exercises.name: Half-Kneeling Bottoms-Up Kettlebell Press

good: Keep the bell balanced straight above the wrist
Feel the shoulder working hard to hold it steady
bad: Don't let the bell tip back over your hand

exercises.note: You've been doing 6 reps here when the card said 8, and then you hit 10 on the 10th. It says 8 now. Stay at 4 kg and own the full eight before you touch a heavier bell.

exercises.name: Chest-Supported Incline Y Raise

good: Chest stays flat on the pad the whole set
Reach the arms up into a Y and feel it low between the shoulder blades
bad: Don't shrug the shoulders toward your ears
Don't lift the chest off the pad to get the arms higher

exercises.note: This is the one you stopped before on Wednesday, and you were right to. Set the bench to about 30 or 45 degrees and lie chest down on it so the pad holds you up instead of your low back. Same job, same weight, same twelve reps. If there is no adjustable bench, do it seated leaning onto your thighs with light cables or a band.

days.completionMessage: Rotation, a controlled pull and the engine, all in one. You did the patient version today and that is exactly what it was meant to be. The bike finish is still the part that shows up in the third set.

good: Easy pace to start
Hips loosening up
bad: Don't start too hard

good: Rotate the hip open, then closed, slowly
Feel the standing glute fighting to hold you
bad: Don't rush it and lose your balance

good: Reach long through the opposite hand and heel
Feel the trunk stay completely still
bad: Don't let the hips rock side to side

good: Step wide against the band
Feel the side of the hip burn
bad: Don't let the knees collapse inward

exercises.name: Medicine Ball Rotational Throw

good: Throw it through the wall, not at it
Feel the back hip drive the turn
bad: Don't throw with the arms and leave the hips behind
Don't hunt for a bigger throw by arching back on the wind-up

exercises.note: Stay on the ball you have been using. No heavier ball this block. Three sets instead of five, and the turn comes from the back hip and the feet, never from the low back. You already rotate all day at work, so this is quality only.

exercises.name: Trap Bar Deadlift

good: Set the chest and take the slack out of the bar before every rep
Feel the legs and glutes start the lift
bad: Don't let the hips shoot up before the bar moves
Don't lean back and lock out hard at the top, just stand tall

exercises.note: I have changed this one. Rebuilding it was the main job of this cycle and that job is now on hold, on purpose. Three sets of five at a 7, controlled up and controlled down, and stay on 20 kg. Stand tall at the top and stop, no leaning back. The heavy version comes back when you have had a clean block, not when your back has a good day. If your back starts talking mid-set, stop this one there and move on to the next exercise. It is not coming off your program.

exercises.name: Machine Leg Press

good: Push the platform away through the whole foot
Feel the thighs fill up
bad: Don't let the hips curl up off the seat at the bottom

exercises.note: Set your depth by your back, not by the machine. The rep ends the moment your hips start to curl up off the seat, and that is your bottom from now on even if the sled has further to go. Short and clean beats deep and rounded.

good: Pull the pad down and under you
Feel the back of the thigh squeeze
bad: Don't let it snap back fast

exercises.name: Banded Dead Bug

good: Press the low back flat into the floor and keep it there the whole set
Feel the deep abs holding while the arm and leg reach away
bad: Don't let the low back lift off the floor as the leg goes down
Don't hold your breath, breathe out as you reach

exercises.note: This one is back, and it is back for your low back. You did every single set of it last cycle without being asked twice. It teaches your ribs and hips to stay stacked so your back stops taking the load your hips should. Only go as far as you can while the low back stays flat on the floor. That range is the exercise.

exercises.name: Assault Bike

good: Go hard enough that the last ten seconds are ugly
Legs and lungs both maxing out
bad: Don't pace it like a steady ride, this is on and off
Don't round over the handles when it gets hard, sit tall

exercises.note: This replaces the whole recovery day you never once did last cycle. Eight rounds, ten minutes, and it is the last thing you do. Any bike works if the air bike is taken. Not the rower though, and not now. Rowing hard when you are already tired is exactly when your back rounds. If every bike is busy, a steep treadmill walk or the stair machine does the same job.

cards.title: Your Low Back, And What To Do With It
cards.body:
You told me about it, and you also told the app on Wednesday when you stopped before the last exercise. That was the right call and I want more of it, not less. Stopping something and writing it down never costs you training with me. It buys you a change, and you just saw one.

Here is what I have changed this week. Nothing has been taken away for good.

  • Day 3 trap bar comes down to three sets of five at a 7, same weight. The heavy rebuild is on hold
  • Throws drop to three sets on the ball you already use
  • Hip thrust loses the squeeze at the top, and the squat holds its weight
  • That last Y raise now happens chest down on a bench instead of on the floor
  • Dead bugs are back on Day 3, because your back likes being braced more than it likes being stretched

You said you want to bend forward and stretch it out. That tells me your back is not enjoying being arched backwards, so everything that finishes in an arch has come off or come down. Keep training. Backs like this get better with movement, not with rest. Walking is good for it. Sitting still all evening is not.

What is normal, and you keep going:

  • Stiffness in the morning that loosens up once you move
  • An ache after a long day on court that has gone by the next morning
  • Normal muscle soreness after a session

What is not, and exactly what to do:

  • Mild and fading: finish the set and write it in the note box that night
  • Building through the set, or changing how you move: stop that exercise. If the card has a smaller version, do that one. If it does not, move on to the next exercise. Write it in the note box either way. Do not wait to ask me first
  • Sharp, or anything going down your leg, or pins and needles: stop the session and message me before the next one

And the hard line, which is not up for discussion. Numbness or pins and needles in either leg, numbness anywhere you sit down on, any change in your bladder or bowel, or a leg suddenly feeling weak. Any one of those and you get seen the same day. Do not message me first. Same if pain starts waking you at night.

You are getting it looked at anyway. Book it by Friday 11 September and send me the date. Booking it is in your hands, being seen quickly might not be. And whatever they say, we are reviewing this together in mid October either way, even if it has been quiet for weeks by then.

cards.title: Both Of Them Are Closed
cards.body:
In your very first session of the last block you logged both knees at 5 out of 10. Two days later it was your right shoulder at 6 and your left at 5. Since then, thirteen sessions, and not one word about either.

That didn't happen by accident. You did the jumps every single Day 1, six for six. You did the shoulder work every single Day 2, four for four, including on the two days you rated the session a 9 out of 10. You never skipped the boring stuff, and that's exactly why it worked.

So they're both signed off. The bounding in this cycle and the pressing on Day 2 are things you've earned back, not things I'm hoping you get away with.

cards.title: Why Your Squat Never Moved
cards.body:
Ten weeks, same weight, every session. And your effort rating on it climbed from a 7 to an 8 to a 10 on the last heavy set, and then you dropped the weight. That's not you stalling, that's the program stalling you.

Five reps with a three second lowering is brutal. You were hitting the effort target long before the bar was ever heavy enough to grow on. So all three barbell lifts change shape this cycle:

  • Squat goes to 3 reps at normal speed, so the weight has room to climb
  • Trap bar was going to 4 reps to rebuild what it lost, and that is now on hold while your back settles. Five controlled reps at a 7 instead
  • Landmine press goes to 5 each side, one point harder

Your job doesn't change. Hit the reps at the effort on the card and log it honestly. If a set lands under the target, the next one goes up. If it grinds above it, stay there another week. Dropping the weight on a bad day isn't failing, it's reading the room.

cards.title: Your Upper Back On Heavy Weeks
cards.body:
This one is your upper back, between the shoulder blades, and it is a separate thing from your low back. It never shows up in your session logs because it isn't a gym problem, it's a court problem. Hours of serving and overheads and your upper back gives out. So Day 2 is built around it now. Pulling volume has doubled and pressing is deliberately low. Face pulls, rows, Y raises. That work is the treatment, not the cause.

What's normal: a burn between the shoulder blades during the pulls, and stiffness the next day. Tightness after a long day of playing that's gone by morning. Keep training through all of that.

What isn't normal, and what to do about it:

  • Mild and fading: finish the set, write it in your log
  • Building through the set, or changing how you move: stop that exercise. Do the smaller version if the card has one, otherwise move on to the next one, and message me
  • Sharp, or going down your arm, or pins and needles: stop the session and message me before the next one

And a hard line: if you get night pain, lose rotation range, get any numbness, or the ache starts arriving earlier week to week, you're seeing a physio, no matter how you feel about it. We review this together at the end of the cycle either way.

cards.title: Three Days, And Why
cards.body:
Four days hasn't happened once. You did 13 sessions out of 20 last block, and Day 4 you never opened, not a single time. That's not a discipline problem, it's a diary problem. So the fourth day is gone and the conditioning moved onto the end of Day 3.

Three days you actually do beats four you don't. Nothing has been thrown away, it's just packed tighter, and every session now finishes inside an hour instead of the 80 or 90 minutes some of yours were running.

On a bad day, the rule stands: drop every effort target by one point and cut the last exercise. And if you've only got half an hour, do the first power move and the first main lift. That counts as the session, and I'd much rather have that than nothing.

You can also move the days around your week. Just keep at least one day between Day 1 and Day 3, they both hammer your legs. On a heavy week on court, take it out of Day 1 or Day 3, never Day 2. Day 2 is the one protecting your upper back.

cards.title: Sleep Is What's Capping You
cards.body:
Your readiness scores through the last block averaged 2.8 out of 5, and sleep alone was 2.7. You rated your sleep a 2 or worse on four of the nine days you filled it in. Meanwhile your effort rating on the same weights climbed a whole point.

That's not your training being too hard. That's you turning up already tired. The gym is not the thing holding you back right now, sleep is.

You don't need a perfect routine. Pick one thing and hold it for the five weeks: same bedtime every night, or the phone out of the room, or no coffee after 2pm. One. Then tell me at check-in whether it moved your readiness number, because that number is the honest scoreboard here.

cards.title: Don't Skip The Bike
cards.body:
Conditioning has quietly disappeared from your training. You did zero conditioning sessions in the whole of the last block. Zero. For a tennis player that shows up in the third set, not in the gym.

So it's now eight rounds on the bike at the end of Day 3, thirty seconds hard and sixty easy. Ten minutes, and it's the last thing you do, so it can't eat into your lifting.

It's on the bike on purpose and not the rower. Rowing hard at the end of a session is exactly when your upper back would start rounding, and that's the thing we're trying to fix.
